(p-147)
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surat al-Ikhlas (The Chapter of Sincerity)

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ *Al-Ahad* (the One). Al-Qurtubi said: That is, the Singular, the Odd, who has no likeness, no equal, no consort, no offspring, and no partner. (End of quotation.)

It is known that all of these meanings are true with regard to Him, the Exalted.

The root of *ahad* is *wahad*, and the *waw* was changed into a *hamza*.

From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*As if my saddle, when the day had passed us by at Dhi al-Jalil, was upon a beast that felt at home, and a lone one (wahad)*

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said, regarding *ahad*, there are two opinions:

The first: that it has the meaning of *wahid* (one).

Al-Khalil said: It is permissible to say, "*Ahad* [is] two, three," and then he mentioned that its origin is *wahad*, and the *waw* was changed into a *hamza* for lightness.

The second: that *wahid* and *ahad* are not synonymous names.

Al-Azhari said: Nothing is described with *ahadiyyah* (oneness of uniqueness) except Allah, the Exalted. One does not say, "a man *ahad*" or "a dirham *ahad*," as one says, "a man *wahid*," meaning single, alone with respect to himself. Rather, *ahad* is one of the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, which He has singled out for Himself, so nothing shares it with Him.

Then he said: They have mentioned several points of difference between *wahid* and *ahad*:

One of them: *wahid* is included in *ahad*, but *ahad* is not included in it.

The second: if you say, "No one [single] can withstand so-and-so," it is permissible to say, "But two can withstand him," unlike *ahad*.

(p-148)
For if you say, "No one (*ahad*) can withstand so-and-so," it is not permissible to say, "But two can withstand him."

The third: *wahid* is used in affirmation, and *ahad* is used in negation.

You say in affirmation, "I saw one man (*rajulan wahidan*)."

And you say in negation, "I did not see anyone (*ahadan*)," which conveys generality.

As for what he transmitted from al-Khalil, which the author of al-Qamus also related, he said: "*Rajul wahid* and *ahad*," that is, contrary to what al-Azhari said.

As for his saying that *ahad* is used in negation, its use in affirmation has also occurred, as in His saying: ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾ [al-Nisa: 43].

So its predominance in usage and the clarity of its indication of generality is evident.

In *Mu'jam Maqayis al-Lughah*, under the section of the *hamza* and the *ha* and what follows them, he said: *Ahad* is a branch, and the origin is the *waw*: *wahad*.

He mentioned it under the *waw* and under the root *w-h-d*. He said: The *waw*, the *ha*, and the *dal* are one root that indicates singularity. From this is *al-wahdah* (with a *fatha* on the *waw*), which is the sole one of his tribe when there is none like him among them. He said:

*O sole one of the Arabs, who has no equal among the people*

It was said that this verse belongs to Bashshar, praising Uqbah ibn Muslim, or to Ibn al-Mawla Yazid ibn Hatim, as transmitted from *al-Aghani*.

Thus it has been established that the original form with the *waw* and the *hamza* is derived from it.

It has already been mentioned that its indication of generality is clearer, that is, *ahad*.

The noble verse indicates that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is *ahad*, that is, in His essence and His attributes, with no likeness, no partner, no equal, and no rival to Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

Its explanation is implicitly given by His saying: ﴿and there is none comparable to Him, [anyone]﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4].

(p-149)
And His saying: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. As for the general meaning, the whole Qur'an, the entire Muhammadan message, and indeed all the messages, came only to establish this meaning: that Allah, glory be to Him, is One, *Ahad*. Indeed, everything in existence bears witness to this.

As it has been said:

*And in everything there is a sign for Him that indicates that He is the One*

As for the texts of the Qur'an on this, they are more than can be counted, because they carry the meaning of *la ilaha illa Allah* (there is no god but Allah).

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, previously made a reference to this at the beginning of *al-Saffat* and elsewhere, and in al-Baqarah: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163].

And in al-Tawbah: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship one God; there is no deity except Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31], so it came connected with *la ilaha illa Allah*.

And in Sad, His saying: ﴿Say: I am only a warner, and there is no deity except Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Sad: 65].

And as we have already stated, the whole message came to establish this meaning, as in His saying: ﴿This is a notification for mankind, and that they may be warned thereby and know that He is but one God﴾ [Ibrahim: 52]. Glory be to Him, exalted is His majesty, sanctified are His names, and transcendent are His attributes. He is One, *Ahad*, in His essence, in His names, in His attributes, and in His actions.

The Qur'an has established this meaning by reason as it has established it by transmission, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods, as they say, then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted far above what they say, a great exaltation﴾ [al-Isra: 42-43].

And His saying: ﴿If there had been in them [the heavens and the earth] gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22].

So it indicates that they are not ruined by the absence of their multiplicity, and He combined reason and transmission in His saying: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there is not with Him any god. [If there were], each god would have took away what he created, and some of them would have exalted themselves over others. Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91].

(p-150) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge (al-Samad)﴾.

Some of the exegetes said: what follows it explains it: ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3].

Ibn Kathir said: this is a good meaning.

Some of the scholars said: al-Samad is the one who has reached the utmost in lordship (al-su'dud) and in perfection in every respect.

It was also said: al-Samad is the one to whom creatures turn (yasmudu) in their needs, while He Himself needs no one.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, had already discussed the meaning of al-Samad in Surat al-An'am, at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'am: 14], and he mentioned the evidence for all of these sayings.

By careful reflection on a beginning that is explained by what follows it, it becomes clear that the whole surah is an explanation of its opening, ﴿Say: He is Allah, One (Ahad)﴾, because oneness (al-ahadiyyah) is His being singled out, glorified be He, with all the attributes of majesty and perfection; and because the one who is begotten is not "one" (ahad), since he is a part of his father.

And the father is not "one", since a part of him is in his son.

Likewise, whoever has an equal (kufu') is not "one", because of the existence of the equal.

Thus the whole surah serves to establish ﴿Say: He is Allah, One﴾.

(p-151) The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾.

The shaykh, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him and on us, has already explained its evidences when commenting on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, who has not taken a son and has no partner in the dominion﴾ [al-Furqan: 2], in Surat al-Isra'.

Caution (tanbih)

Taking a son does not necessarily entail the negation of begetting, because taking a son may occur without begetting, as in adoption (tabanni) or otherwise. This is shown in the story of Yusuf, in the words of Allah, the Exalted, about the ruler of Egypt: ﴿Honour his residence; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son﴾ [Yusuf: 21].

In this surah there is therefore a more specific negation, so it was necessary to draw attention to it in this noble surah, which is Surat al-Ikhlas (p-151). It is the surah that equals one third of the Qur'an, because it is specific to the right of Allah, the Exalted, in His essence and attributes: His oneness (wahdaniyya), His self-sufficiency (samadiyya), the negation of begetting and being begotten, and the negation of any equal. All of these are attributes of Allah's exclusive singularity, glory be to Him.

In it there is an explicit text that He, glory be to Him and exalted, did not beget and was not begotten. So it is more specific than the other negations. This is among the matters established for all Muslims without doubt, dispute, or any disagreement affecting it.

However, non-Muslims did not accept this. The Jews said: ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾, the Christians said: ﴿The Messiah is the son of Allah﴾, and the polytheists said: the angels are the daughters of Allah.

They agreed on claiming a son for Allah, but no one claimed that He, glory be to Him, was begotten.

Explicit texts have indeed come negating a son for Allah, glory be to Him and exalted. Yet the mere text which the opponent does not believe in is not sufficient to persuade him. In this surah, which is specific to the attributes of Allah, there is no mention of what prevents Allah from taking a son and from being begotten, glory be to Him.

Since stating the preventing factor or the necessitating factor is part of the method of this book, whenever a ruling has a necessitating or preventing factor and no reference to it has been made earlier, then in what preceded from the shaykh's speech, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him and on us, although he, may Allah have mercy on him, spoke about the verses of the Names and Attributes in general and in detail in a way that suffices and heals, [it was not made explicit].

But the Noble Qur'an mentions the claim that Allah has a son, exalted is He far above that by a great elevation.

Allah's reply came together with the statement of the preventing factor in detail, along with an indication of the rational proof, and therefore it was necessary to draw attention to it. This is in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And they say: Allah has taken a son. Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him. The Originator of the heavens and the earth; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116-117].

This is an explicit text regarding what they said: ﴿Allah has taken a son﴾.

(p-152) And it is an explicit text declaring Allah, glory be to Him, free of what they said and glorifying Him.

Then the particle of retraction (harf al-idrab) came against their saying: ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾. In it is a rational statement of the preventing factor against taking a son, by what binds the opponent. The ultimate purpose of taking a son is that he be dutiful to his father, and that the father benefit from his son, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 46]. Or the son is an heir to his father, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted, about His prophet Zakariyya, peace be upon him: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾ [Maryam: 5-6].

Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is the Living, the Everlasting, who inherits and is not inherited, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Everything upon it will perish, but there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 26-27].

And His words: ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 180].

So if everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, in devout submission and obedience, willingly or unwillingly, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is not befitting the Most Merciful that He should take a son. There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a slave﴾ [Maryam: 92-93].

Then He, glory be to Him and exalted, is not in need of a son, because He is free of need of it.

Then He, glory be to Him, showed His power over origination and innovation in His words: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117].

This is clear in negating a son from Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

He praised Himself in His words: ﴿And say: Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has no partner in the dominion, and has no protector out of weakness; so magnify Him with full magnification﴾ [al-Isra': 111].

As for His not being begotten: no one claimed this of Him, because it is rationally impossible, by the known argument from mutual dependence, which is as follows.

If His existence, glory be to Him, depended on His being begotten, then in His existence He would need someone to bring Him into existence; and then the one who begets Him would himself need a parent, and so on, leading to circularity (dawr) and infinite regress (tasalsul), and this is invalid.

(p-153) Likewise, the need for a son, by its negation, implies the meaning of self-sufficiency (samadiyya) already mentioned. If He had a parent, the parent would be prior and more deserving [of divinity], exalted is Allah far above that.

It may also be said, from the side of rational impossibility, if it is supposed as in His words: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of those who worship﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81].

We say, on this supposition: if He had a son, what is the origin of this son's existence and what is his end? If he is originated, when did his origination occur? If he is eternal, then eternity would be multiplied, and this is impossible.

Then, if he is everlasting, permanence would be multiplied; and if he is finite, when is his end?

And if his ultimate fate is to end, what is the need to bring him into existence when there is no need for him? Thus the taking of a son is negated by reason and by transmitted text, just as begetting is negated in the same way, by reason and by transmitted text.

Some exegetes raised a question about this verse: why did it put the negation of a son before the negation of begetting, although the usual order in what is observed is that one is begotten and then begets?

They answered that this is from placing what is more important first, because it is a refutation of the Christians in their saying "Isa is the son of Allah", of the Jews in their saying: ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾, and of the polytheists' saying: the angels are the daughters of Allah. And because no one claimed that He, glory be to Him, was begotten by anyone, their claim that Allah has a son is a monstrous slander. End of quotation.

As Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but a lie﴾ [al-Kahf: 5].

And His words: ﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son. Certainly you have produced a monstrous thing. The heavens nearly rend from it, the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin, that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son﴾ [Maryam: 88-91].

Because of the enormity of this slander, He mentioned it first, then refuted its impossibility with His words: ﴿It is not befitting the Most Merciful that He should take a son. There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a slave﴾ [Maryam: 92-93].

We have already presented the proof of prevention by reason and by transmitted text.

(p-154) Here there is another question: if the claim of a son has occurred, and the refutation came against it, then the claim of begetting has not occurred, so why was its negation mentioned when no one claimed it?

The answer, and Allah the Exalted knows best: whoever permits for Him begetting and that He have a son, may also permit that He be begotten. So the negation of begetting came to complete the negation and the declaration of His transcendence, just as in the hadith of the sea: the question was only about performing ablution with its water, so the answer covered its water and its dead creatures, because what allowed the question about its water allows doubt about its dead creatures. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

(p-155) The words of the Exalted: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾. They said: *kufu'an*, *kufuwan* and *kafa'an* all have one meaning, which is "equal" (*al-mithl*).

The statements of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) on the meaning of the verse are many, but all of them revolve around the negation of likeness.

From Ka'b and 'Ata': He has no equal and no peer.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it means: "There is nothing like Him."

From Mujahid: that is, He has no consort.

The negation of *kufu'* (equal), *mithl* (like), *nidd* (rival) and *'adl* (equivalent) has all come in the Qur'an. *Kufu'* is in this surah, *mithl* is in His words ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ and His words ﴿So do not strike forth similitudes for Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 74].

*Nidd* is in His words ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22].

*'Adl* is in His words ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

Our Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, had already given an explanation of this at the verse of al-An'am: they make others equal to Him from *al-'idl* (with the first letter vowelled with a kasra), which is one of the two halves of a camel's load according to one of the two interpretations. The other meaning is from *al-'udul* (turning away) from Him to other than Him.

There are two topics that the exegetes raise regarding this surah. The first is its occasions of revelation (*asbab al-nuzul*), and the second is what has been related about its virtues. It was not within the scope of this book to trace these, except for what has a connection to the meaning.

(p-155) As for what has been related about its virtues, Abu Hayyan said in his tafsir: "The exegetes have greatly multiplied the citing of narrations on this, and this is not its place." He was right in what he said. Ibn Kathir, al-Fakhr al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, and Ibn Hajar in *al-Isaba*, in the biography of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and others have cited them, but this is not the place to cite them. The exception is what has come in the Sahih, that its recitation equals a third of the Qur'an, because its subject matter is connected to *tawhid* (the affirmation of Allah's oneness).

As for the other topic, the occasion of its revelation, it has been said: the polytheists asked the Prophet ﷺ to describe his Lord for them, so it was revealed.

His words within it, ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾, are a refutation of attributing offspring to Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

A similar meaning occurred when Pharaoh asked Moses about his Lord, and he said to him: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 23].

So the answer came: ﴿[Moses] said: "The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you were certain."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said to those around him: "Do you not listen?"﴾ ﴿[Moses] said: "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said: "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 24–27].

I had heard from our Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, that the reason for Pharaoh's saying of Moses "mad" is that Moses had been asked with *ma* in Pharaoh's words ﴿Pharaoh said: "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"﴾. *Ma* is used to ask for the explanation of the quiddity (*sharh al-mahiyya*), so the question with it required that he explain the quiddity of the Lord, glory be to Him, of what He is made, just as one answers "What is man?" with "He is a rational animal."

But Moses, peace be upon him, turned away from Pharaoh's question, either out of ignorance of the reality of Allah, or out of feigned ignorance, as in His words: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. He answered him with what was specific to him and what he must acknowledge: that He, glory be to Him, is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, not the false lordship of Pharaoh.

Similar to this in the Qur'an: when they asked about the crescent moons, "What is the matter with them, that they appear small and then grow?" It is a question about the reality of their change, so the Qur'an left aside answering their question as they asked it, and answered them with what binds them and benefits them.

Likewise was the answer of the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), peace be upon him, to Nimrod when he disputed with him about his Lord: ﴿When Abraham said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258].

(p-156) He mentioned Him, glory be to Him, by His attributes. In this surah, when they asked about the reality of Allah and His lineage, the answer came with His attributes, because what they were asking about applies only to created things, not to the Creator, glory be to Him, and to the possible, not to the Necessarily Existent in Himself (*wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi*). Glory be to Him whose essence none but Himself comprehends. And Allah the Mighty spoke truly in His words: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11], and ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, while they do not encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Taha: 110].

(p-157) The two protecting surahs: Surat al-Falaq and Surat al-Nas

The exegetes report from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to regard them as two protective surahs not part of the Qur'an. But Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: "I bear witness that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed me that Jibril, peace be upon him, said to him: ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak﴾ [al-Falaq: 1], so I said it, and he said ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 1], so I said it. So we say what the Prophet ﷺ said." Ibn Kathir cited this from Imam Ahmad, and he cited something similar from al-Bukhari, then said: "Then he returned from his view to the view of the majority, for the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, recorded them in the mushafs of the leading cities and sent them out to all regions." It is also narrated from Imam Ahmad that the Prophet ﷺ recited them in prayer, and he cited several chains proving that they are Qur'an, which removes any dispute after that regarding their affirmation. Al-Qurtubi offered an excuse for Ibn Mas'ud: that he had not heard them from the Prophet ﷺ as Qur'an, and when he heard them he thought they were supplications among the supplications, like the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from the evil of what He created." When it reached him that the Prophet ﷺ had affirmed them, he returned to the view of the majority.

It is worth mentioning the connection between these two and the preceding Surat al-Ikhlas. When He, glory be to Him and exalted, mentioned that He is the One, the Unique (*al-Ahad*), the Single (*al-Fard*), the Eternal Refuge (*al-Samad*), and *al-Samad* among its meanings is that toward which creatures turn in their needs, these two surahs came directing the servants to the One they seek refuge with and take shelter in, who is Allah, the Eternal Refuge, glory be to Him. He alone is the One who protects them and guards them, and He is the One to whom they turn for refuge, glory be to Him.

His words ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak﴾ amount to seeking refuge with the Creator from what He created, because everything that is split open is split by something other than itself, except Allah, the One who neither begets nor is begotten.

The second after it is ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind﴾, the God of mankind. Allah willing, there will come a note on what the context indicates regarding the ending of the blessed mushaf with these two noble surahs, and the comparison between them to show the greatness of their rank. Our Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, had also referred to Surat al-Nas to complete the discussion of the singling out of Allah in worship, as we will fully clarify, Allah willing, in its place. And success is from Allah the Exalted.
